extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, scholars and policy-makers interested in freedom of expression, satire and religion-related controversies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and contextual criteria relevant to producing, publishing, and evaluating satirical cartoons (especially those referencing religion), including legal limits, editorial judgement, cultural sensitivities, and security considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of expression vs legal restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of speech in Denmark is quite far-reaching ... although it is subject to some legal restrictions dealing with libel, hate speech, blasphemy and defamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and commentators must account for statutory limits (libel, hate speech, blasphemy, defamation) when exercising free expression; national norms on expression (e.g., Denmark's comparatively lenient approach) influence how controversial material is treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 140 (insulting legal religions) — historical criminal provision
rubrics_metrics.description: At the time, section 140 of the Danish Penal Code criminalized mocking or insulting legal religions and faiths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although section 140 was rarely used (no convictions since 1938 reported then) and was repealed in 2017, publishers should be aware that laws criminalizing religious insult have existed and may affect prosecutorial decisions or public response; a complaint under §140 was filed against Jyllands-Posten but the prosecutor declined to file charges, citing freedom of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 266 b (hate speech) — penalisation of hateful public utterances
rubrics_metrics.description: Utterances intended for public dissemination deemed hateful based on 'race, colour, national or ethnic origin, belief or sexual orientation' can be penalised under section 266 b of the criminal code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material that targets protected groups (e.g., Muslims) may be prosecutable under hate-speech provisions; historically some people have been convicted under this provision for speech directed at Muslims—publishers should assess whether cartoons 'undermine' or vilify a group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecutorial balancing of offence vs free expression
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing what constitutes an offence under both section 140 and section 266 b ... the right to freedom of expression must be taken into consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers (prosecutors, courts) explicitly weigh freedom of expression against alleged offence/hate; creators and publishers should anticipate that legal outcomes may hinge on that balancing test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial discretion to reject offensive submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Jyllands-Posten rejected unsolicited cartoons in 2003 which depicted Jesus on the grounds that they were offensive... In February 2006, Jyllands-Posten refused to publish Holocaust cartoons offered by an Iranian newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may and do exercise discretion to refuse material considered offensive; consulting affected communities or authorities (e.g., the main rabbi was consulted before publishing some Holocaust cartoons) is an editorial practice used to gauge acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and security considerations for publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Yale University Press refused to publish the cartoons and other representations of Muhammad out of fear for the safety of its staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers weigh staff safety and potential violent reprisals when deciding whether to print contentious images; such considerations can override purely editorial or principled arguments for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-censorship versus political correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: The cartoons were first printed in response to the perception of some journalists at the newspaper that self-censorship was becoming a problem... Rose: 'this act was about self-censorship, not free speech.' He also highlighted a difference between political correctness and self-censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators and newsrooms should distinguish between voluntary restraint (political or ethical choices) and fear-driven self-censorship; the latter is presented as more problematic because it arises from intimidation rather than considered judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious tradition (aniconism) and depiction norms
rubrics_metrics.description: The Qur'an condemns idolatry... This has led major Islamic scholars and legal schools to prohibit figurative representation; for mainstream Islamic scholars, all pictorial representations of Prophets are prohibited... images of Muhammad have been made on many occasions, generally in a restricted and socially regulated way; for example, they are often stylised or do not show Muhammad's face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding Islamic aniconism and the variety of local practices is essential when depicting religious figures; historically acceptable conventions (stylisation, not showing the face) reduce perceived sacrilege in many communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insulting Muhammad as a particularly severe cultural offence
rubrics_metrics.description: In Muslim societies, insulting Muhammad is considered one of the gravest of all crimes. The Islamic sharî'a has traditionally considered blasphemy punishable by death, although modern Muslim thinkers ... maintain that the Quran does not prescribe a punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where legal penalties vary, creators should recognise that depictions perceived as insulting Muhammad carry extremely strong cultural and emotional reactions, and may provoke severe social and political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical intent and specific associations increase offence
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the BBC, 'It is the satirical intent of the cartoonists and the association of the Prophet with terrorism, that is so offensive to the vast majority of Muslims.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The combination of ridicule/satire and linking a religious figure to violent or criminal themes (e.g., terrorism) magnifies offensiveness; intent and framing matter for public reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for content to create marginalisation and intimidation (hate speech reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is reasonable to consider two of the cartoons as hate speech... [They] create a social environment of conflict and intimidation for a community that already feels that its way of life is threatened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should consider whether images contribute to a hostile environment that marginalises a community; such social harms are arguments used to classify material as hate speech beyond purely abstract notions of offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accusations of racism and essentialising religion as identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some argued the cartoons were racist because Muslims are in practice treated as a group based on their religion, and the cartoons were intended to represent all of Islam and all Muslims in a negative way, not just Muhammad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether material is racist versus critical of ideas, consider whether it essentialises adherents as a monolithic group and attributes negative characteristics to them collectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double standards and comparative legal-political consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: There were claims of double standards in defending free speech for these cartoons while outlawing Holocaust denial; critics argued such discrepancies raise questions about consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of policy or editorial stances should assess consistency across similarly offensive expressions (e.g., treatment of Holocaust denial vs religious satire) to avoid perceptions of hypocrisy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and geopolitical framing
rubrics_metrics.description: The incident occurred at a time of unusually strained relations between parts of the Muslim world and the West... many commentators argued the reaction was used by different political interests in a wide variety of local and international situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of controversial publications should factor in broader historical and geopolitical contexts (immigration, recent conflicts, domestic politics) and recognise that reactions may be shaped or amplified by those contexts or actor interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of controversy as a political tool by various actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commentators believed that the controversy was used by Islamists competing for influence ... Other regimes in the Middle East have been accused of taking advantage of the controversy ... to demonstrate their Islamic credentials, distracting from their domestic situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that responses to publications may be orchestrated or exploited by political actors for electoral or domestic legitimising purposes; motive and coordination can affect interpretation of the scale and nature of reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial stance and political alignment influence content
rubrics_metrics.description: Jyllands-Posten has been described as conservative ... anti-Islamic positions and discourse dominated Jyllands-Posten's editorial leadership from at least 2001 until the cartoon crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A news outlet's political orientation and prior coverage patterns should be considered when evaluating its commissioning or publication of provocative material; perceived agenda-setting affects credibility and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative precedent and proportionality of responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The following incidents are often compared to the cartoon controversy: The Satanic Verses controversy, Charlie Hebdo, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the appropriateness of publishing or responding to satire, compare to precedent cases (scale of offence, legal outcomes, level of violence) to assess proportionality and possible consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of governmental investigations and judicial codification
rubrics_metrics.description: These government investigations of journalists catalysed debate about the role of government in censoring or prosecuting expressions they deemed potentially hateful. Critics said the cartoon controversy was a sign that attempts at judicial codification of such concepts as respect, tolerance and offence have backfired on the West.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about relying solely on legal codification of offence/tolerance; heavy-handed government intervention in matters of expression can prompt backlash and complex debates about rights and limits.
